principles.name: The ball decides your job (centre of play)

summary.standard: Where the ball is decides what you should be doing. Defending, the nearest player presses, the next one covers and everyone else keeps the shape; attacking, the carrier goes forward, nearby players support and the rest give width and depth.
summary.kid: The ball tells you your job: go to it, back up, or hold your spot.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Rank players by distance to the ball. Defending: the nearest is the 1st defender (press or delay); the next teammate who is goal-side and within about 15 m (default) is the 2nd defender (cover); everyone else is a 3rd defender (balance, compactness). Attacking: the carrier is the 1st attacker; teammates within 12 m (default) of the ball are 2nd attackers (support); the rest are 3rd attackers (width, depth). The published 9.15 m radius comes from 3v3 games, so 12 m is our 11v11 guess.

why.standard: If two players go to the ball and nobody covers, one pass beats both of them, so knowing your job instantly keeps the team organised.
why.kid: If two of you chase the ball, nobody backs up. One pass beats you both. Know your job and do it fast.

principles.commonMistake: Everyone near the ball chases it at once, leaving no cover and no balance behind.

learnMore.label: U.S. Soccer Coaching Curriculum 2011 (free PDF)
FUT-SAT: ten core tactical principles (open-access paper)

principles.name: Shift with the ball as a unit

summary.standard: Your spot is not fixed: as the ball moves, the whole team slides with it, and every role has a home position for each ball position.
summary.kid: When the ball moves, the whole team slides with it.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Your target follows the ball: a base spot blended from stored ball positions, or roughly anchor + k x (ball - centre). Measured slopes from HELIOS data (along / across the pitch): back line about 0.5 / 0.3, #6 0.70 / 0.47, #8 0.80 / 0.40, wingers 0.72 / 0.25, #9 0.71 / 0.43 (measured). So a back-liner moves about half as far as the ball does lengthways.

why.standard: A team that slides together keeps its gaps small wherever the ball goes; a player who stays put opens a hole the opponent can play through.
why.kid: Slide with the ball as one team. That keeps the gaps small. Stand still and you open a hole they can play through.

principles.commonMistake: Treating your formation spot as if it were painted on the grass instead of sliding when the ball changes side.

learnMore.label: Coaches' Voice: football tactics explained

principles.name: The team pushes up with the ball and drops without it

summary.standard: When your team has the ball, the whole block moves further up the pitch; when you lose it, the block moves back toward your own goal.
summary.kid: Got the ball? Everyone moves forward. Lost it? Everyone moves back.

principles.ruleOfThumb: On top of your ball-based spot, shift about 6 m (default) toward their goal in possession and about 4 m (default) toward your own goal out of possession.

why.standard: Pushing up puts more players near their goal and squeezes space; dropping back protects the space behind you when the other team can play forward.
why.kid: Step forward together and their space shrinks. Move back together and you guard the space behind you. Move as one, both ways.

principles.commonMistake: Defenders staying deep while the team attacks, which stretches the team and leaves a huge gap in midfield.

learnMore.label: Coaches' Voice: football tactics explained

principles.name: Offside (hard rule)
principles.who: Attackers, and the back line that sets the line

summary.standard: You are in an offside position if, when a teammate passes, you are in their half and closer to their goal line than both the ball and their second-last player. Being level counts as onside.
summary.kid: When the pass is played, don't be past their last defender.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Offside position = in the opponent half (x > 52.5) and nearer their goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent (the keeper is usually the last). Head, body and feet count; hands and arms do not. Level is onside. There is no offside offence straight from a goal kick, throw-in or corner. The app allows a 0.3 m (default) margin before it calls offside.

why.standard: An offside run kills the attack and hands the ball back; timing your run to stay level keeps the threat alive.
why.kid: An offside run kills the attack. Stay level with their last defender and your run stays dangerous.

principles.commonMistake: Drifting past the last defender while waiting for the pass, instead of staying level and running when the ball is played.

learnMore.label: IFAB Laws of the Game: Law 11, offside

principles.name: A space is yours if you get there first

summary.standard: A spot belongs to whichever team can reach it first, so a good position is one you can get to before an opponent, not just one that looks empty.
summary.kid: A space is yours only if you get there first.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Arrival time is about 0.7 s to react plus distance / 5 m/s, after carrying your current run on for 0.7 s; the ball travels at about 15 m/s. Control of a spot is shared out by who arrives sooner (a smooth pitch-control model, sourced from Spearman).

why.standard: Space an opponent reaches first is not really free, so reading arrival times tells you which passes and runs will actually work.
why.kid: Free space is only free if you get there first. Watch who arrives first. Then you know which runs and passes will work.

principles.commonMistake: Moving into space that looks empty but that a nearby defender can close before the ball arrives.

learnMore.label: Spearman et al. 2017: modelling pass probabilities (PDF)

principles.name: Scan before you move

summary.standard: Look over your shoulders several times before the ball comes to you or before you move, so you already know where teammates, opponents and space are.
summary.kid: Look around before the ball comes, so you know what's there.

principles.ruleOfThumb: At least 3 scans in the roughly 10 s before you receive or reposition; midfielders aim for at least 0.4 scans per second. Scan earlier when pressure is coming, because scanning drops once a defender is close.

why.standard: Players who scan more complete more forward passes, because they have chosen their next move before the ball arrives.
why.kid: Look around before the ball comes. Then you already know your next move. Players who look more pass forward more.

principles.commonMistake: Watching only the ball, so you miss the runner behind you or the free teammate beside you.

learnMore.label: Jordet et al. 2020: scanning in the Premier League (paper)

principles.name: Predict the likely next pass

summary.standard: Before you pick a spot, work out what the player on the ball is most likely to do next, then position for that while still guarding the most dangerous option.
summary.kid: Guess where the next pass will go, then get ready for it.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Read the carrier's open passing lanes, body shape and pressure to pick their likeliest next action. Position for the likeliest threat while still covering the most dangerous one.

why.standard: Expert players anticipate instead of reacting, which buys them the half-second that decides who gets to the ball.
why.kid: Great players spot what happens next before it happens. That half second decides who gets the ball.

principles.commonMistake: Reacting only once the pass has been played, which is always a step too late.

learnMore.label: Roca et al. 2011: how expert players anticipate (paper)

principles.name: Keep sensible spacing

summary.standard: Stay far enough from teammates that one opponent can't mark two of you, but close enough to help each other.
summary.kid: Don't stand too close to a teammate, or too far away.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Nearest teammate 6-18 m away (HELIOS median 11.4 m, 10th-90th percentile 6.2-16.8 m, measured). Never stand where a single opponent can guard both you and a teammate.

why.standard: Bunched players are easy to mark and easy to press, while stretched players can't support or cover each other.
why.kid: Bunched players are easy to guard. One defender can watch two of you. Spread out so you can help each other.

principles.commonMistake: Drifting toward the ball until you are standing next to a teammate who is already there.

learnMore.label: U.S. Soccer Coaching Curriculum 2011 (free PDF)

principles.name: Width: make the field big

summary.standard: In possession, the widest player on each side stays close to the touchline, which stretches the defence and opens gaps between their players.
summary.kid: When we have the ball, someone stays wide near the sideline.

principles.ruleOfThumb: The widest player on each side is within 0-5 m (default) of the touchline (y < 5 or y > 63). When the ball is on the other wing, the far winger still stays wide instead of drifting into the half-space.

why.standard: Width forces the defence to spread out, which opens passing lanes through the middle and gives you a switch of play.
why.kid: Stay wide and their defenders must spread out. That opens paths through the middle. It also sets up a long pass to the other side.

principles.commonMistake: Drifting inside toward the ball, so the team becomes narrow and easy to squeeze.

learnMore.label: US Youth Soccer ODP Player Manual (free PDF)
U.S. Soccer Coaching Curriculum 2011 (free PDF)

principles.name: Depth: pin their back line

summary.standard: The striker stays on the last defender's shoulder, which pushes their defence back and stretches the space between their lines for teammates.
summary.kid: Striker: stay level with their last defender, ready to run.

principles.ruleOfThumb: The #9 stays within 0-2 m (default) of the second-last defender's line on the onside side, never beyond it while in their half and ahead of the ball (that is offside, F4). Once the ball itself is past their line, fill the box instead (P10).

why.standard: A striker on the shoulder threatens the ball in behind, so their defenders can't step up and your midfield gets room between the lines.
why.kid: Stand on their last defender's shoulder. They must stay back or you run in behind. Your midfield gets more room.

principles.commonMistake: Dropping deep for the ball too often, which lets their back line push up and squeeze the space.

learnMore.label: US Youth Soccer ODP Player Manual (free PDF)

principles.name: Support: always 2+ passing options

summary.standard: The player on the ball should always have at least two teammates to pass to, at different angles and heights, with no defender in the passing lane.
summary.kid: Get where a pass can reach you, with no defender in the way.

principles.ruleOfThumb: At least 2 teammates with a clear lane: no opponent within 1.5-2 m (default) of the pass line. Options at different heights and widths, at least 30 degrees apart (default). Never stand directly behind a defender on the line from the ball to you. From v2, a lane counts as open when the interception model gives P_lane > 0.6.

why.standard: With two open options the carrier cannot be trapped; with one or none, a single presser can win the ball.
why.kid: Give the player with the ball two open choices. Then they cannot be trapped. With none, one chaser can win the ball.

principles.commonMistake: Standing behind a defender, where the carrier can't pass to you even though you look free.

learnMore.label: U.S. Soccer Coaching Curriculum 2011 (free PDF)
Touchline Theory: a practical guide to positional play

principles.name: Support distance depends on pressure

summary.standard: If the carrier is free and facing forward, stay further away to stretch the play; if they are under pressure or facing their own goal, come closer to offer a short, safe pass.
summary.kid: The more trouble on the ball, the closer you come.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Carrier unpressured and facing forward: support from 12-25 m (default), holding width or height, or running in behind. Carrier pressed (an opponent within about 3 m) or facing their own goal: players ahead come short to 5-10 m (default).

why.standard: A pressed player needs a quick short pass to escape, while a free player needs longer options that get past opponents.
why.kid: A teammate in trouble needs a short, quick pass. A free teammate can use a longer one that gets past opponents.

principles.commonMistake: Coming short to a teammate who is free and facing forward, which crowds them and takes away the long pass.

learnMore.label: U.S. Soccer Coaching Curriculum 2011 (free PDF)

principles.name: Lanes and lines

summary.standard: Spread out across the five vertical lanes and across different horizontal lines, so the team never has too many players in one channel or one row.
summary.kid: Spread out so the team fills more of the pitch.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Lane edges at y = 0 / 13.84 / 24.84 / 43.16 / 54.16 / 68. At most 2 teammates per vertical lane and at most 3 on one horizontal line (sourced), treating +/- 2.5 m (default) as the same line. If your lane or line is full, move to the next one.

why.standard: Players in different lanes and lines create diagonal passing angles and force defenders to choose whom to mark.
why.kid: Stand in a different path and row from your teammates. Passes can go diagonally. Defenders must pick who to watch.

principles.commonMistake: Moving into the same lane as a teammate, so one defender can cover both of you.

learnMore.label: Touchline Theory: a practical guide to positional play
Spielverlagerung: tactical analysis and glossary

principles.name: Fullback and winger share the flank
principles.who: The full-back and winger on the same side

summary.standard: The full-back and winger on one side should not stand in the same strip of pitch: if one holds the touchline, the other moves inside, and the other way round.
summary.kid: Only one of you stays wide; the other comes inside.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Never both in the wing lane within about 10 m (default) of each other. If the winger hugs the touchline, the full-back comes inside (the half-space, or next to the #6). If the full-back overlaps, the winger moves into the half-space.

why.standard: Two players in one lane can be marked by one defender; splitting them stretches their full-back and opens the half-space.
why.kid: Two of you in one path is easy to guard. Split up and their full-back cannot watch both. A gap opens just inside the wing.

principles.commonMistake: The full-back overlapping into the space the winger is already holding.

learnMore.label: Spielverlagerung: tactical analysis and glossary
Touchline Theory: a practical guide to positional play

principles.name: Peel off and open your body

summary.standard: Move away from your marker so they are not between you and the ball, and open your body toward their goal so your first touch can go forward.
summary.kid: Step away from your defender and face their goal when you receive.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Get your marker out of the line between you and the ball. Keep your body at least 45 degrees (default) open toward their goal. Avoid receiving with your back to goal when a marker is within 2 m (default).

why.standard: Receiving open lets you see the whole pitch and play forward straight away instead of being forced backward.
why.kid: Get open before you receive. Then you can see the pitch and play forward right away. No one forces you backward.

principles.commonMistake: Standing still behind your marker and receiving with your back to goal.

learnMore.label: US Youth Soccer ODP Player Manual (free PDF)

principles.name: Circulate and switch
principles.who: Centre-backs, the #6, full-backs and far-side players

summary.standard: Move the ball quickly and, when one area gets crowded, switch it to the other side, where far-side players should already be wide and open.
summary.kid: If one side is crowded, move the ball to the other side.

principles.ruleOfThumb: After 2-3 short passes in one zone, the next pass should leave that zone. A back pass is usually followed by a switch, so far-side players are already wide and free. Prefer a diagonal pass to a straight pass into a tightly marked teammate.

why.standard: Switching play makes the defence shift across the pitch, and if it can't shift fast enough, gaps open on the far side.
why.kid: A long pass to the other side makes their whole team run across. If they are slow, gaps open on the far side.

principles.commonMistake: Far-side players drifting toward the ball, so there's nobody wide to switch to.

learnMore.label: US Youth Soccer ODP Player Manual (free PDF)

principles.name: Salida lavolpiana against a front two

summary.standard: Against two pressing strikers, the #6 drops between the centre-backs to make a back three, the centre-backs split wide and the full-backs push high.
summary.kid: Two strikers chasing? The midfielder who stays back comes between the defenders.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Only against a front two: the #6 drops between the CBs, the CBs split to about y 14 and y 54, and the full-backs push high and wide. Against a single striker, the #6 stays in front of the CBs.

why.standard: Three builders against two pressers always leaves one player free to carry or pass forward.
why.kid: Three of you against two chasers always leaves one of you free. The free one can carry or pass forward.

principles.commonMistake: The #6 dropping in every time, even against one striker, which leaves midfield empty.

learnMore.label: The Outfield: the salida lavolpiana explained

principles.name: Goal-kick shape

summary.standard: At a goal kick the centre-backs split to the corners of the box, the #6 shows in the middle and the full-backs go wide, giving the keeper several short options.
summary.kid: At a goal kick, spread out so the keeper can pass to you.

principles.ruleOfThumb: The ball is in play once it is kicked and moves, and teammates may receive inside the box; opponents must stay outside the box until then. CBs at the box corners (x about 5-16, y about 14 and 54), the #6 central at x about 18-25, full-backs wide (y < 5 or y > 63) at x about 15-35 (all defaults).

why.standard: A spread shape makes the opponent choose whom to press and gives the keeper a safe first pass.
why.kid: Spread out and they must choose who to chase. Your keeper always has a safe first pass.

principles.commonMistake: Everyone crowding near the keeper, so one presser can cover several options.

learnMore.label: US Youth Soccer ODP Player Manual (free PDF)

principles.name: The keeper supports the build-up

summary.standard: The goalkeeper moves to give the centre-back a safe back pass, changing distance and side so the passing line stays clear of the presser.
summary.kid: Keeper: move so a defender can always pass back to you.

principles.ruleOfThumb: If the ball-side CB is within about 10 m of the keeper, the keeper moves to the far half of the box to make passing distance; if the CB is far away, the keeper comes toward the ball side. Keep the CB-to-GK pass line at least 1.5 m (default) from the presser.

why.standard: A keeper who is always available turns pressure into an extra free player for your team.
why.kid: A keeper who is ready for a pass is an extra free player. Use them when you are stuck.

principles.commonMistake: The keeper staying in the middle of the goal line, where the back pass is either too short or blocked.

learnMore.label: FIFA Training Centre: the goalkeeper in and out of possession

principles.name: Offensive unity: the back line follows the attack

summary.standard: As your team moves the ball forward, the defenders move up too, so the team stays connected instead of stretching.
summary.kid: When we attack, defenders move up too, so the team stays together.

principles.ruleOfThumb: As the ball advances, the last line advances too, so its distance to the ball doesn't grow. In possession, keep the back line 35-45 m (default) from the front line.

why.standard: A connected team can win the ball back quickly after losing it and gives the attack more passing options.
why.kid: Stay connected to your teammates. You win the ball back faster. You also give the attack more choices.

principles.commonMistake: Defenders watching the attack from deep, leaving a huge gap for a counter-attack through midfield.

learnMore.label: FUT-SAT: ten core tactical principles (open-access paper)

principles.name: Occupy the half-space
principles.who: The #8, a #10, or an inverted winger or full-back

summary.standard: With the ball in midfield or the final third, get a teammate into the ball-side half-space between their midfield and defence, where their full-back and centre-back can't agree who should mark you.
summary.kid: Stand in the gap between the middle and the wing.

principles.ruleOfThumb: With the ball in the middle or final third, one teammate stands in the ball-side half-space (y 13.84-24.84 or 43.16-54.16), level with or between the opponent's midfield and defensive lines. Their CB or FB must then choose between stepping out and staying.

why.standard: The half-space gives you diagonal views of goal and of both sides of the pitch, and it sits between two defenders' zones.
why.kid: Just inside the wing you can see goal and both sides. You stand between two defenders. Neither is sure who should take you.

principles.commonMistake: Staying in the centre lane with the #9, or drifting wide into the winger's lane.

learnMore.label: Spielverlagerung: tactical analysis and glossary
Coaches' Voice: football tactics explained

principles.name: Receive between the lines, outside cover shadows
principles.who: The #8, a #10, a dropping #9 or an inverted winger

summary.standard: Find space in the gap between their midfield and defensive lines, away from defenders and not hidden behind a presser's back.
summary.kid: Find the gap between their midfielders and their defenders.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Your x lies between the opponent midfield line and their defensive line, at least 3 m (default) from the nearest opponent, with no opponent within 1.5 m (default) of the pass line. If you're in a presser's cover shadow, shuffle 2-4 m sideways out of it.

why.standard: A player who receives between the lines can turn and run at the back line, which is the hardest thing for a defence to handle.
why.kid: Get the ball in the gap behind their midfielders. Turn, and you can run at their defenders. That is the hardest thing to stop.

principles.commonMistake: Standing in a presser's cover shadow, where the pass to you is blocked even though you look free.

learnMore.label: Touchline Theory: a practical guide to positional play
Motzenbecker: the five superiorities

principles.name: The #10 lives in zone 14 or a half-space
principles.who: A #10 (in a 4-3-3, the #8 who pushes up)

summary.standard: The attacking midfielder plays behind their midfield and in front of their defence, either centrally just outside the box or in a half-space, ready to receive half-turned.
summary.kid: Find space just outside their box, behind their midfielders.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Behind the opponent midfield line and ahead of their back line, either in zone 14 (x about 75-88, centre lane) or in a half-space. Receive half-turned. If the #9 checks short, run beyond them.

why.standard: From zone 14 you can shoot, slip a runner in behind or switch play, so defenders have to come to you.
why.kid: In front of their box you can shoot, slip a runner through, or play the other side. Defenders must come to you.

principles.commonMistake: Coming too deep to get the ball, where you are no threat to their goal.

learnMore.label: Coaches' Voice: football tactics explained
Spielverlagerung: tactical analysis and glossary

principles.name: The #8 arrives late

summary.standard: In possession the #8 supports from the half-space, and when the ball goes wide near their box, runs from deep into the box or the cut-back zone after the striker has gone.
summary.kid: Run into the box a moment after the striker, not with them.

principles.ruleOfThumb: In possession, occupy the ball-side half-space between the lines. When the ball goes wide in the final third, run from deep into the box or into the cut-back zone at the edge of it, arriving after the #9.

why.standard: Late runners are hard to track because defenders are already busy with the players in the box.
why.kid: Arrive late in the box. The defenders are busy with the players already there. Nobody is watching you.

principles.commonMistake: Arriving in the box too early, so you're marked and standing still when the cross comes in.

learnMore.label: Coaches' Voice: football tactics explained

principles.name: Runs in behind: when and how

summary.standard: Run in behind only when the passer can actually play the ball forward, and time the run so you stay onside.
summary.kid: Run behind them only when your teammate can pass forward.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Run only when the carrier faces forward and is unpressured, or is pressed but can still play forward. Stay onside at the moment of the pass (F4). Wide runs bend outward; central runs start flat along the line, then bend in behind.

why.standard: A well-timed run turns one pass into a chance, while a badly timed one is offside or never gets the ball.
why.kid: Time your run well and one pass makes a chance. Run too soon and you are offside. Wait, watch, then go.

principles.commonMistake: Running in behind when the carrier is facing their own goal, so the pass can never come.

learnMore.label: US Youth Soccer ODP Player Manual (free PDF)

principles.name: Runs trigger runs
principles.who: The #9 and #10, and the winger and full-back

summary.standard: When a teammate leaves a space by moving toward the ball, the nearest player fills that space quickly, and two runners never aim for the same spot.
summary.kid: When a teammate leaves a space, someone else fills it.

principles.ruleOfThumb: When a teammate checks toward the ball out of a zone, the nearest teammate fills the space within 1-2 s. No two runners target spots within 5 m (default) of each other.

why.standard: A defender who follows the first runner leaves space for the second, but if nobody fills it the run is wasted.
why.kid: When a runner pulls a defender away, space opens. Someone must fill it fast, or the run is wasted.

principles.commonMistake: Watching a teammate's run instead of moving into the space it opened.

learnMore.label: US Youth Soccer ODP Player Manual (free PDF)
U.S. Soccer Coaching Curriculum 2011 (free PDF)

principles.name: Third-man combination

summary.standard: When the direct pass to a runner is blocked, a nearby teammate receives and lays it off first time to the runner, who has moved on the defender's blind side.
summary.kid: If the pass is blocked, go through a teammate who sets it up.

principles.ruleOfThumb: If the pass from A to C is blocked, B offers to receive from A and set it to C. C starts on the blind side of the defender watching B (behind them, more than 3 m away, default) and times the run for B's first touch.

why.standard: Defenders watch the ball and the receiver, so the third player arriving from their blind side is often unmarked.
why.kid: Defenders watch the ball and the first runner. The third player comes from their blind side. Often nobody sees them.

principles.commonMistake: The third player standing still and waiting instead of starting the run as the first pass is played.

learnMore.label: Coaches' Voice: football tactics explained

principles.name: Create a local superiority

summary.standard: Around the ball, aim for an advantage: more attackers than defenders, a free player facing forward between the lines, your best dribbler one-on-one, or a runner who arrives first.
summary.kid: Near the ball, try to have more players than them.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Inside the centre of play: at least one more attacker than defenders (numerical); at least one receiver facing forward between the lines (positional); your best dribbler isolated 1v1 (qualitative); arriving in space before the defender (dynamic).

why.standard: Attacks succeed where you outnumber or out-position the defence, not where you are evenly matched.
why.kid: Attack where you have more players than they do. An even fight is slow. Extra numbers win.

principles.commonMistake: Staying in your zone while a 2v1 near the ball is there for the taking.

learnMore.label: Motzenbecker: the five superiorities

principles.name: Zone 14 is prime real estate

summary.standard: The central area just outside the opponent's box is where many assists start, so getting a player on the ball there, then moving it into the box quickly, is valuable.
summary.kid: The space just outside their box is a great place to get the ball.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Reward getting a player into x about 75-88, y 24.84-43.16, and moving the ball from there into the box quickly (in under about 8 s).

why.standard: From zone 14 a player can shoot, play a through ball or switch, so it stretches every defender at once.
why.kid: In front of their box every choice is open: shoot, pass through, or go wide. Every defender must worry at once.

principles.commonMistake: Holding the ball too long in zone 14 while the defence recovers.

learnMore.label: Spielverlagerung: tactical analysis and glossary
Coaches' Voice: football tactics explained

principles.name: Fill the box on crosses
principles.who: The #9, the far winger and the #8s

summary.standard: When the ball is wide near their byline, attackers spread across the box, near post, back post, penalty spot and the edge for cut-backs, so every kind of cross has a target.
summary.kid: When we cross, fill different spots in the box, not one.

principles.ruleOfThumb: With the ball in a wing lane at x > 88, attackers fill at least 3 of 4 zones: near post (near side of the six-yard box), back post (far side of it), penalty spot (x about 94, y about 34) and the edge of the box (x about 86-89) for cut-backs. No two runners in the same zone, that is within about 3 m (default).

why.standard: Spread runners give the crosser several targets and stop one defender from dealing with two attackers.
why.kid: Spread out for the cross. The crosser gets more targets. One defender can never deal with two of you.

principles.commonMistake: Everyone running to the near post, leaving the back post and the cut-back empty.

learnMore.label: FIFA Training Centre

principles.name: Occupy valuable space, not just free space

summary.standard: The best space to move into is close enough to the ball to receive, controlled by your team, and dangerous if you get the ball there.
summary.kid: Go where you could get the ball and hurt them.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Value of a spot = closeness to the ball (Gaussian, sigma about 14 m) x your team's control of it x its goal threat (EPV). Pick the highest-value spot you can reach in about 2 s, roughly 6.5 m away.

why.standard: Free space far from goal is harmless, so the best runs combine being open with being dangerous.
why.kid: Being free far from goal does not hurt them. The best runs are open and dangerous at the same time.

principles.commonMistake: Running into empty space that is safe but gives the team nothing.

learnMore.label: Fernandez and Bornn 2018: measuring space creation (PDF)
Spearman et al. 2017: modelling pass probabilities (PDF)

principles.name: Commit numbers forward

summary.standard: In settled possession in their half, get enough players ahead of the ball to threaten their goal.
summary.kid: When we attack, get lots of players ahead of the ball.

principles.ruleOfThumb: In settled possession in the attacking half, at least 5 outfield players are ahead of the ball. Fewer than 4 ahead is flagged as a sterile attack.

why.standard: With too few players ahead of the ball the defence can mark everyone and the attack goes nowhere.
why.kid: If too few of you are ahead of the ball, they can watch everyone. The attack goes nowhere.

principles.commonMistake: Too many players staying behind the ball to be safe, so the attack has no targets.

learnMore.label: Coaches' Voice: football tactics explained

principles.name: Rest defence: stay balanced while attacking

summary.standard: While your team attacks, a group of about five players stays at or behind the ball, positioned to stop a counter-attack the moment the ball is lost.
summary.kid: While we attack, some players stay back to stop a fast break.

principles.ruleOfThumb: About 5 players at or behind the ball, in a 3+2 or 2+3. Rest defenders are at least the opponent's forwards + 1. The upper pair blocks the central lanes near the ball; the lower line deals with long balls.

why.standard: Most dangerous counters start the moment you lose the ball, and a prepared rest defence stops them before they begin.
why.kid: The worst breakaways start the second you lose the ball. Keep two players back and ready, and they die early.

principles.commonMistake: Rest defenders standing level with each other far from the ball, so one pass goes past all of them.

learnMore.label: Coaches' Voice: football tactics explained

principles.name: Counter-press after losing the ball
principles.who: The 2-4 players nearest the ball when it is lost

summary.standard: The moment you lose the ball, the nearest players press it straight away while teammates block the short passes; if it isn't won back within a few seconds, drop into shape.
summary.kid: Lost the ball? Chase it right away for a few seconds.

principles.ruleOfThumb: The nearest player, within about 10 m (default), presses immediately; the next nearest block short passes and mark the outlets. It works best in the first 2-3 s; stop at about 5 s. If the press is bypassed or the ball isn't won, retreat into a compact block.

why.standard: Right after a turnover the opponent is disorganised and often facing the wrong way, so it is the best moment to win the ball back.
why.kid: Right after they win the ball, they are not set. Many face the wrong way. Chase right away: it is the best time to win it back.

principles.commonMistake: Pressing alone while teammates jog back, so one simple pass escapes the press.

learnMore.label: Spielverlagerung: tactical analysis and glossary
Coaches' Voice: football tactics explained

principles.name: Delay the counter: drop and narrow

summary.standard: If you can't win the ball back straight away, or you're outnumbered, back off toward your goal and squeeze toward the middle to slow the attack until help arrives.
summary.kid: Can't win the ball? Back off and slow them down.

principles.ruleOfThumb: If you can't pressure the ball, or you're outnumbered, retreat toward goal and narrow toward the centre lane. Keep more defenders than attackers between the ball and goal. The defender facing the carrier backs off, keeping 3-5 m (default), to slow them and show them wide.

why.standard: Every second you delay lets teammates recover, while diving in against a numbers advantage lets the attack through.
why.kid: Can't win it? Slow them down. Every second lets teammates run back. Diving in against more players lets them through.

principles.commonMistake: Diving in to tackle when outnumbered, so one touch takes the carrier past you.

learnMore.label: The FA England DNA: out of possession

principles.name: Recovery run: get goal-side
principles.who: Anyone caught ahead of the ball

summary.standard: When the ball goes past you, sprint back toward your own goal, not toward the ball, until you're goal-side of both the ball and your opponent.
summary.kid: Ball got past you? Sprint back toward your goal, not the ball.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Run on a line toward your own near post or the goal centre, not toward the ball, until you are goal-side of the ball and your opponent. Then rejoin the line or press the carrier from behind.

why.standard: Chasing the ball from behind rarely wins it and leaves the space in front of goal open, while getting goal-side puts you back between the ball and the net.
why.kid: Chasing from behind rarely wins the ball. Get back between the ball and your goal first. Then you can stop the attack.

principles.commonMistake: Chasing the ball on a curved path instead of running back toward your own goal first.

learnMore.label: U.S. Soccer Coaching Curriculum 2011 (free PDF)

principles.name: Prepare the counter before you win the ball

summary.standard: When a teammate is about to win the ball, players not involved in the tackle already move between the lines or start runs in behind, ready for a forward pass.
summary.kid: Teammate about to win it? Get ready to run forward.

principles.ruleOfThumb: When a teammate is about to win the ball, players not involved stop defending and take diagonal positions between the opponent's lines or start runs in behind. The first pass after the regain goes forward if a runner is free.

why.standard: The opponent is most disorganised in the seconds after losing the ball, so being ready first turns a tackle into a chance.
why.kid: They are most open just after they lose the ball. Be ready first and a tackle becomes a chance.

principles.commonMistake: Still standing in your defensive position after your team has won the ball.

learnMore.label: U.S. Soccer Coaching Curriculum 2011 (free PDF)

principles.name: First defender: pressure the ball

summary.standard: The defender nearest the ball closes the carrier down quickly, then slows down and stops just goal-side of them, blocking the way to goal.
summary.kid: Nearest to the ball? Go close, stay between it and our goal.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Close down fast, then slow down with short steps. Stop 1.5-3 m (default) away, goal-side, on or near the line from the ball to the centre of your goal (within 20 degrees when play is central, default). Stand side-on.

why.standard: Pressure takes away the time to look up and pass forward, and it forces mistakes.
why.kid: Go close fast and they have no time to look up. No time means no forward pass. Rushed players make mistakes.

principles.commonMistake: Running straight in and diving in, so the carrier simply goes around you.

learnMore.label: Minnesota Youth Soccer: defending coaching points (PDF)
U.S. Soccer Coaching Curriculum 2011 (free PDF)

principles.name: Dictate direction: show them outside
principles.who: The first defender, and the whole press

summary.standard: Approach at an angle that shuts the middle and leaves only the route toward the nearest touchline, where the sideline acts like an extra defender.
summary.kid: Block the middle so they can only go toward the sideline.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Curve your approach so the central lane is shut and the open side faces the nearest touchline (or the carrier's weaker foot). With the ball in a wing lane, stand on the inside of the line from the ball to your goal.

why.standard: Play pushed wide is far from goal and easy to trap, while play allowed inside can go straight at goal or be switched.
why.kid: Send them wide, away from goal. Wide play is easy to trap. Let them inside and they can go straight at goal.

principles.commonMistake: Approaching straight on, so the carrier can go either way, including inside toward goal.

learnMore.label: Minnesota Youth Soccer: defending coaching points (PDF)
Coaches' Voice: football tactics explained

principles.name: Second defender: cover at an angle

summary.standard: The second defender stands diagonally behind the presser, close enough to step in if the carrier gets past and far enough inside to protect the goal.
summary.kid: Stand behind your teammate at a slant, ready if they're beaten.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Goal-side of the presser on a diagonal, 3-6 m behind and 2-4 m inside (defaults). Closer (3-5 m) when play is central and near goal; further (6-10 m) when it is wide and far away. Never level with the presser and never directly behind them. Sit a little further inside when the ball is near the touchline. On a square pass, the two defenders swap jobs.

why.standard: If the presser is beaten, the cover player is already in position to stop the attack before it reaches goal.
why.kid: If your teammate chases and is beaten, you are already behind them. You stop the attack before it reaches goal.

principles.commonMistake: Standing level with the presser, so one pass beats you both, or directly behind them, so one dribble does.

learnMore.label: Soccer Coach Weekly: what is covering?

principles.name: Balance: the weak side tucks in

summary.standard: Players far from the ball move toward the middle so the team protects the dangerous central area, accepting that the far touchline is left open.
summary.kid: Far from the ball? Move toward the middle to help.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Players more than about 25 m (default) sideways from the ball move toward the centre, and the team's average position shifts toward the ball. In the centre of play, defenders goal-side of the ball at least match the attackers. A far-side attacker can be left free while the carrier is under pressure.

why.standard: The ball can't be switched instantly, so far-side space is less urgent than the central space near the ball.
why.kid: The ball cannot jump across the pitch in a flash. Guard the middle near the ball first. The far side can wait.

principles.commonMistake: Staying wide to mark a far-side winger, leaving a big gap between you and the nearest defender.

learnMore.label: U.S. Soccer Coaching Curriculum 2011 (free PDF)

principles.name: Goal-side and ball-side marking

summary.standard: When marking, stand between your opponent and the centre of your goal, a little toward the ball, so you can see both and reach a pass first.
summary.kid: Stay between your player and our goal, and watch the ball.

principles.ruleOfThumb: On the line from your opponent to the centre of your goal, 1-3 m from them (tighter nearer goal) and shifted 1-2 m toward the ball (defaults). Your x must be smaller than theirs. Keep your body open so you can see the ball and your opponent.

why.standard: A defender on the wrong side can only chase, while a goal-side defender can intercept and is never beaten by a simple ball in behind.
why.kid: On the wrong side you can only chase. On the goal side you can step in and take the ball. Nothing in behind beats you.

principles.commonMistake: Marking from the side or in front, so one pass in behind leaves your opponent clean through.

learnMore.label: U.S. Soccer Coaching Curriculum 2011 (free PDF)

principles.name: Cut off the return pass
principles.who: Any defender who has just been bypassed by a pass

summary.standard: After a pass goes past you, first step into the line of the likely return pass, then chase the ball.
summary.kid: Beaten by a pass? Block the pass back first, then chase.

principles.ruleOfThumb: First recover into the lane between the passer and the receiver's return option; then chase the ball.

why.standard: The quickest way through a defence is a one-two, and blocking the return pass kills it.
why.kid: The fastest way through is a quick one-two. Stand where the return pass would go and you kill it.

principles.commonMistake: Turning and chasing the ball at once, so the passer runs off you for the return.

learnMore.label: Soccer iQ by Dan Blank (book)

principles.name: Zonal defending: hand over, take over

summary.standard: In a zonal system, defend your area: when an attacker leaves your zone, pass them on to the teammate whose zone they're entering instead of following them.
summary.kid: Runner leaving your area? Let the next teammate take them.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Reference order: ball, then space, then teammates, then opponent. When an attacker leaves your zone, pass them on to the teammate whose zone they enter. Man-mark only the most dangerous runner near your box, or when a zone-mate has been beaten.

why.standard: Following every runner drags the shape apart, while handing over keeps the team compact.
why.kid: Follow your runner everywhere and the shape rips open. Hand them over and stay. The team stays tight.

principles.commonMistake: Following your attacker all over the pitch and leaving your zone empty.

learnMore.label: Spielverlagerung: tactical analysis and glossary

principles.name: Pressing triggers

summary.standard: Jump to press together on a cue such as a back pass, a heavy touch or a receiver facing their own goal, and otherwise hold your shape.
summary.kid: Chase together when they pass back or make a mistake.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Triggers: a back pass, a heavy touch, a receiver facing their own goal, a pass to a full-back near the touchline, the keeper on the ball, a slow or looped pass, or a square pass across their back line. On the trigger, the nearest player engages, the next blocks the nearest option and the rest squeeze up. No trigger: hold your shape. Only jump if someone can cover behind you.

why.standard: Pressing together at the right moment wins the ball high up the pitch, while pressing at random just gets you bypassed.
why.kid: Chase together at the right moment and you win the ball high. Chase alone at random and they just pass around you.

principles.commonMistake: Pressing on your own without a trigger, so the rest of the team isn't ready to follow.

principles.name: Cover shadow and curved pressing runs

summary.standard: While pressing, run on a curve so your body blocks the pass to the most dangerous player behind you, cutting out an option as you close the ball down.
summary.kid: Curve your run to the ball so your body blocks the pass behind you.

principles.ruleOfThumb: While pressing, stay within 1.5 m (default) of the line from the carrier to the most dangerous receiver behind you, somewhere 15-90% of the way along it. Curve your run so your shadow cuts the inside pass: for example, the #9 presses a CB from the inside to cut the pass to the other CB or the #6.

why.standard: A presser who also blocks a passing lane does two jobs at once, so fewer players are needed to press.
why.kid: Chase the ball along the line of a pass. You do two jobs at once. Fewer teammates need to leave their spots.

principles.commonMistake: Running straight at the ball, which leaves the easy pass behind you wide open.

Coaches' Voice: football tactics explained

principles.name: Compactness: stay short and narrow

summary.standard: Out of possession, keep the distance from the deepest to the highest player small and the team narrow, so there are no big gaps to pass through.
summary.kid: Stay close together as a team so there are no big gaps.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Outfield length (deepest to highest) at most 35 m, about 25 m in a pressing block (HELIOS median 31 m, measured). Gap between the defence and midfield lines about 12-15 m (40-50 ft, sourced). Block width at most about 50 m (measured). Don't open a gap of more than 15 m to your own line.

why.standard: A compact team leaves no space between its lines, so the opponent has to play around it rather than through it.
why.kid: Stay tight as a team, front to back. There is no space through you. They must go the long way around.

principles.commonMistake: Defenders dropping deep while midfielders press, which opens a big hole between the lines.

Coaches' Voice: football tactics explained

principles.name: Shift and slide, no crossover
principles.who: The back line and the midfield line

summary.standard: Move across the pitch together with even gaps between neighbours, and never swap places with the teammate beside you; hand runners over instead.
summary.kid: Slide across as a team and keep the same gaps between you.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Neighbours keep roughly equal gaps: about 8-12 m near the ball and wider on the far side (a tolerance band, not a target; defaults). When shifting, never cross your nearest teammate; hand the runner over. No gap should be wide enough for a through ball.

why.standard: Uneven gaps are where through balls go, and crossing over leaves your own space empty.
why.kid: Keep the gaps even. Uneven gaps are where through balls go. Crossing over leaves your own space empty.

principles.commonMistake: Following a runner across your teammate's path, which leaves a hole where you were.

principles.name: Line height: step, hold or drop

summary.standard: The back line steps up when the ball goes backward or the carrier is pressed and facing away, holds while the ball is under pressure, and drops when the carrier is free to play forward.
summary.kid: When the ball goes backward, your whole line steps forward.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Step up about 5 m (default) when the ball goes backward, or when the carrier is pressed and facing away. Hold when the ball is under pressure. Drop 5-10 m (default) when the carrier is unpressured and facing forward.

why.standard: An unpressured passer facing forward can play in behind a high line, while stepping up at the right moment squeezes space and catches attackers offside.
why.kid: Their passer free and facing you? Stay back. Their passer rushed? Step forward together and catch runners offside.

principles.commonMistake: Holding a high line while the carrier has time and space to play a ball in behind.

learnMore.label: Coachbetter: how the back four behaves

principles.name: A level line, set by the CB nearest the ball

summary.standard: The back line stays level with the centre-back nearest the ball, except for a deliberate covering drop, so nobody keeps an attacker onside.
summary.kid: Defenders stay in a straight line, so nobody keeps a striker onside.

principles.ruleOfThumb: The other defenders stay within +/- 1-2 m (default) of the x of the centre-back nearest the ball, except for a deliberate covering drop. A deep far-side defender who keeps an attacker onside is a critical fail.

why.standard: One defender a few metres deeper than the rest plays every attacker onside and ruins the offside line.
why.kid: Stay level with your defenders. One player standing behind the rest keeps every attacker onside. That ruins the trap for everyone.

principles.commonMistake: The far-side defender dropping deeper than the line and keeping an attacker onside.

learnMore.label: Coachbetter: how the back four behaves

principles.name: Back-four shape with the ball wide

summary.standard: When the ball is wide, the near full-back engages, the near centre-back covers, the far centre-back narrows and the far full-back tucks in, forming a crescent or an L-shape.
summary.kid: Ball out wide? The defenders slide across and close the gaps.

principles.ruleOfThumb: The near FB engages the winger; the near CB covers diagonally; the far CB narrows toward the near CB; the far FB tucks in to within 10-15 m (default) of the far CB. A crescent (far FB deepest) or an L (far CB deepest) are both fine. No gap of more than 12 m (default) between neighbouring defenders near the ball.

why.standard: Protecting the side of the box and the middle at once needs the back four to move as one shape, not as four individuals.
why.kid: Move as one line of four. Then the middle and the sides are guarded at once. Four players doing their own thing guard nothing.

principles.commonMistake: The far full-back staying wide, leaving a big gap between them and their centre-back.

learnMore.label: Coachbetter: how the back four behaves
Trainerblog: back-four spacing and shifting (German)

principles.name: Block height: high, mid, low
principles.who: The whole team, including the goalkeeper

summary.standard: A team defends in a high, mid or low block depending on where it sets its lines, and each block has its own heights for the defence and the front line.
summary.kid: We defend high up, in the middle, or low near our box.

principles.ruleOfThumb: High: CBs near halfway (x about 45-52, sourced), strikers on their CBs and keeper. Mid: front line near halfway, back line at x about 25-35; block central passes and let them play wide. Low: back line near the edge of the box (x about 16-22), two narrow, compact banks. Every figure except the high-block one is a default.

why.standard: Everyone has to defend at the same height, because one player in a different block breaks the whole shape.
why.kid: Defend at the same height as everyone else. One player too high or too low breaks the whole shape.

principles.commonMistake: Strikers pressing high while the defence sits in a low block, leaving a huge space in between.

principles.name: Concentration: protect the scoring area
principles.who: Centre-backs, full-backs, the #6 and the weak-side winger

summary.standard: When the ball is in your defensive third, players away from the ball squeeze toward the centre, between the ball and goal, to protect the area where goals are scored.
summary.kid: Ball near our goal? Everyone moves into the middle to guard it.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Ball in your defensive third: off-ball defenders shift toward the centre, between the ball and goal. The weak-side full-back tucks in to about the width of the box, at or inside the far-post line. Never leave the lane from the ball to the penalty spot open while guarding empty space out wide.

why.standard: Most goals come from central areas close to goal, so that is the space you must fill first.
why.kid: Most goals come from the middle, close to goal. Fill that space first. The corners can wait.

principles.commonMistake: Staying wide with a far-side winger while the space in front of goal is empty.

principles.name: Defend crosses
principles.who: Centre-backs, the far full-back, the #6 or #8, and the goalkeeper

summary.standard: When the ball is wide near your box, someone pressures the crosser, the centre-backs protect the goal, the far full-back joins at the back post and a midfielder guards the cut-back.
summary.kid: When they cross, guard the goal, the back post and the edge.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Someone pressures the crosser. The CBs stay central, between the posts (y 30.34-37.66) and inside the box. The weak-side full-back joins the line near the far post, goal-side of the runner. A midfielder covers the penalty spot or the edge of the box for cut-backs. Protect the width of the goal first.

why.standard: Crosses are dangerous because attackers run onto the ball, so defenders who hold central positions have to meet it first.
why.kid: A cross is dangerous because attackers run onto it. Hold the middle and you meet the ball first.

principles.commonMistake: Centre-backs being dragged to the near post by a run, leaving the middle of the goal open.

learnMore.label: U.S. Soccer Coaching Curriculum 2011 (free PDF)
Coaches' Voice: football tactics explained

principles.name: The centre-back pair

summary.standard: The two centre-backs work as a pair: in possession they split wide to build, and out of possession one sets the line while the other covers, never too far apart.
summary.kid: Centre-backs: one goes to the ball, the other backs them up.

principles.ruleOfThumb: In possession: split to about the width of the box when the #6 drops or at goal kicks, and carry the ball into space when not pressed. Out of possession: the CB nearest the ball sets the line (U4); the partner covers 3-6 m behind and inside (default); stay within about 12 m of each other (default); stay central on crosses.

why.standard: A centre-back pair that drifts apart leaves a gap in the most dangerous channel, while a pair that covers each other can take risks.
why.kid: Centre-backs guard each other. Drift apart and a gap opens right in front of goal. Stay a pair and you can take risks.

principles.commonMistake: Both centre-backs stepping to the same attacker, so nobody is covering.

learnMore.label: Coachbetter: how the back four behaves

principles.name: The fullback out of possession

summary.standard: With the ball on your side, engage the winger and show them outside with your centre-back covering; with the ball on the far side, tuck in toward your centre-back and stay level.
summary.kid: Ball on the far side? Come in beside your centre-back.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Ball on your side: engage the winger goal-side and force them outside, with the CB covering. Ball on the far side: tuck in to within 10-15 m (default) of your CB and stay level with the line. Recovery runs go toward the near post first.

why.standard: The full-back's position decides whether the back four has a gap on the far side or a winger running free on the near side.
why.kid: Ball far away? Come in beside your centre-back, or a gap opens. Ball on your side? Meet the winger or they run free.

principles.commonMistake: Staying wide on the far side while the ball is on the other flank.

learnMore.label: Coachbetter: how the back four behaves

principles.name: The #6 screens the centre-backs

summary.standard: Out of possession the holding midfielder stays central, just in front of the centre-backs, blocking passes into the most dangerous attacker.
summary.kid: Defensive midfielder: stay in the middle, in front of your defenders.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Out of possession, stay in the centre lane 5-10 m ahead of the CBs (HELIOS median 7.3 m, measured; up to 15 m allowed, default). Sit on or near the line from the ball to the most dangerous central attacker. Don't get pulled wider than the half-space unless you are covering.

why.standard: The #6 blocks the passes that split the centre-backs, and without them the opponent can play straight through the middle.
why.kid: The player in front of your defenders blocks the passes that would split them. Without that, they play straight through the middle.

principles.commonMistake: Chasing the ball out wide and leaving the space in front of the centre-backs empty.

learnMore.label: Spielverlagerung: tactical analysis and glossary
Coaches' Voice: football tactics explained

principles.name: Winger duties

summary.standard: In possession, stay high and wide near the touchline unless the full-back is holding the width; out of possession, get goal-side of their full-back quickly.
summary.kid: Attacking: stay wide and high. Defending: get back to their full-back.

principles.ruleOfThumb: In possession: high and wide, within about 5 m (default) of the touchline, especially as the far-side winger. Only come inside if the full-back holds the width (B6). Out of possession: get goal-side of the opposing full-back quickly. In a high press, curve inside-out to shadow the CB-to-FB pass.

why.standard: The winger stretches the defence in attack and stops their full-back from overlapping in defence.
why.kid: Hug the sideline. In attack you stretch their defence. In defence you stop their full-back running past you.

principles.commonMistake: Drifting inside to find the ball, which crowds the middle and removes the team's width.

learnMore.label: US Youth Soccer ODP Player Manual (free PDF)

principles.name: Striker duties

summary.standard: In possession, play on the last defender's shoulder; when pressing, lead the press and block the pass between their centre-backs; on crosses, attack the near post or the penalty spot.
summary.kid: Stay on their last defender, chase first, and attack crosses in the box.

principles.ruleOfThumb: In possession: on the last defender's shoulder, onside (B2); check short only to open space for a runner. Pressing: you are the first line of pressure; curve your run so your shadow cuts the CB-to-CB or CB-to-#6 pass (D9). Crosses: attack the near post or the penalty-spot zone (P10).

why.standard: The #9 sets the height of the opponent's defence and the direction of your team's press.
why.kid: Your striker decides how high their defenders dare stand, and where your team starts to chase.

principles.commonMistake: Dropping deep for the ball all the time, which leaves nobody to run in behind.

learnMore.label: US Youth Soccer ODP Player Manual (free PDF)
Coaches' Voice: football tactics explained

principles.name: Angle and depth

summary.standard: Stand on the line that splits the angle between the ball and your two posts, and come further off your line the further away the ball is.
summary.kid: Keeper: line up between the ball and the middle of your goal.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Stand on the line that bisects the angle between the ball and the two posts. Depth off the line by ball distance: ball 27-32 m from goal gives 3-5 m; ball at halfway (about 52 m) gives about 11 m; ball in their box puts you at or beyond the top of your own box, about 16.5 m (sourced). More than 1 m (default) off the bisector when a shot is possible is a fail.

why.standard: The right angle and depth cover the most goal with the fewest steps and let you sweep up balls played over the top.
why.kid: The right angle and the right distance guard most of the goal with few steps. You can still race out for a ball over the top.

principles.commonMistake: Staying on the goal line or hugging the near post, which leaves a big part of the goal open.

learnMore.label: Keeperstop: how far off the line should the keeper be?

principles.name: The 3-metre rule

summary.standard: If the attacker on the ball is very close, go low and wide to block; if they are further away and in control, stay tall and set rather than charging.
summary.kid: Close attacker? Go low and wide. Far away? Stay big and still.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Carrier within 3 m: go low, wide and square to block or smother, showing them away from goal. Beyond 3 m: stay tall and set, narrow the angle along the bisector and do not charge. Moving more than 2 m (default) toward a controlled carrier who is over 3 m away counts as rushing.

why.standard: Charging a composed attacker lets them chip or round you, while staying set makes them beat you with a perfect shot.
why.kid: Charge out wildly and they chip you or go around you. Stay set and they must beat you with a perfect shot.

principles.commonMistake: Rushing out at an attacker who has the ball under control.

learnMore.label: FIFA Training Centre: the goalkeeper in and out of possession

principles.name: Starting position for crosses

summary.standard: When the ball is wide in your third, the keeper's starting spot moves from just in front of the near post when the ball is close to the byline toward the middle of the goal when it is far out, and deeper for deep crosses.
summary.kid: Cross coming? Keeper: start near the post if close, middle if far.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Sideways: from one step in front of the near post (ball near the byline beside the box) to the middle or back third of the goal (ball 30 m or more from the goal line). Depth: 0.5-1.5 m off the line for close or in-swinging deliveries; 2-5 m for deep or out-swinging ones, or when the crosser is on the end line (defaults).

why.standard: A good starting spot lets you cover a near-post shot and still come out to claim a cross.
why.kid: Start in the right spot. You can save a shot at the near post and still come out for a cross.

principles.commonMistake: Standing in the middle of the goal when the crosser is close to the near post, inviting a near-post shot.

principles.name: Sweeper-keeper: stay connected to the line

summary.standard: With a high defensive line, the keeper stays connected to it, moving up and back so they can sweep up balls played in behind.
summary.kid: Our defenders are high? Keeper moves up behind them.

principles.ruleOfThumb: With a high line, stay 15-25 m (default) behind the last defender and move up and back with the line. This conflicts with G1's depths when the block is high, so the app uses G4 for a high block and G1 otherwise.

why.standard: A high line leaves space in behind, and a keeper who is off their line can clear through balls before an attacker reaches them.
why.kid: When your defenders stand high, space opens behind them. Stand off your line, and you can clear a through ball first.

principles.commonMistake: Staying on the goal line behind a high back line, leaving acres of space for a through ball.

principles.name: Defending free kicks: the wall

summary.standard: Size and line up the wall according to where the free kick is, anchored on the line to the near post, while the keeper covers the far side.
summary.kid: Free kick near our box? Build a wall ten big steps from the ball.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Wall size: 5 when central within about 7 yd of the edge of the box; 4 at 20-25 yd, just off centre; 3 at 25-30 yd, wider; 2 when wide. Anchor it on the line from the ball to the near post, 9.15 m from the ball, extending toward the goal centre. The keeper covers the far half, starting between the goal centre and the far post, about 1 m (default) off the line. Attackers must stay at least 1 m from a wall of 3 or more.

why.standard: A well-placed wall takes away the near side, so the keeper only has to cover one half of the goal.
why.kid: A good wall blocks one side of the goal. The keeper only has to guard the other half.

principles.commonMistake: Lining the wall up with the middle of the goal, which blocks the keeper's view and leaves the near post open.

principles.name: Defending corners: zonal
principles.who: All ten outfield players and the goalkeeper

summary.standard: In a zonal corner, each defender guards an area in and around the six-yard box rather than a player, and attacks the ball if it comes into that area.
summary.kid: At corners, guard your area and attack any ball that comes in.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Own goal at x = 0, corner taken from the y = 0 side. The keeper commands the six-yard box; one player stands about 1 m inside the near post. Zones: front-post space (x about 3-5, y about 27-31); three six-yard-line zones (x about 5.5, y about 30 / 34 / 38); back-post space (x about 3-5, y about 40-42); one on the line from the near post to the penalty spot; the penalty spot itself (x about 11, y about 34); and the edge of the box (x about 16.5-18) for second balls. All coordinates are defaults.

why.standard: Zones make sure the most dangerous spaces are always filled, whatever runs the attackers make.
why.kid: Guard the spaces, not the runners. The danger spots are always filled, whatever runs they make.

principles.commonMistake: Leaving your zone to follow a runner, which opens the space the ball is aimed at.

principles.name: Defending corners: man-to-man and mixed

summary.standard: Markers stay goal-side of their attacker, touch-tight and open to the ball; a mixed system combines a few zonal players on the six-yard line with markers on the best headers.
summary.kid: At corners, stay between your player and the goal, very close.

principles.ruleOfThumb: A marker stands goal-side, on the attacker's line to the goal centre, within about 1 m, with an open body. Mixed system: 3-4 zonal players on the six-yard line; the best headers mark the 3-4 most dangerous attackers; one player protects the keeper; 1-2 hold the edge of the box. No system was clearly better at the 2022 World Cup, so the app scores against the system each scenario declares.

why.standard: Tight goal-side marking stops attackers getting a free run at the ball.
why.kid: Stay tight, between your player and our goal. Then they never get a free run at the ball.

principles.commonMistake: Marking from in front of or beside your attacker, so they run past you to the ball.

principles.name: Attacking corners: fill the zones, keep rest defence

summary.standard: Send at least three attackers into different zones, offer the taker a short option, and leave enough players back to stop a counter.
summary.kid: At our corners, spread out in the box and keep some players back.

principles.ruleOfThumb: At least 3 attackers arrive in different zones: near post, central six-yard box, back post, penalty spot, and the edge of the box for cut-backs, no two within about 3 m (default). A 'train' of 4-6 players around the spot with one blocker is an option. Offer a short option to the taker. Keep rest defenders at least the opponent's outlets + 1; outlets usually wait at the edge of the box or near post.

why.standard: Spread runners give the taker a target in every zone, and a rest defence stops a cleared corner turning into a goal against you.
why.kid: Spread out so the taker has a target in every part of the box. Keep two back so a cleared ball cannot become their goal.

principles.commonMistake: Sending everyone forward, so a cleared corner becomes a breakaway.

principles.name: Throw-ins
principles.who: The full-back or winger on the throw side, the #8 and the #9

summary.standard: Give the thrower at least three options, short to feet, down the line and back inside, and remember there is no offside from a throw-in.
summary.kid: Throw-in: give short, long and back options. No offside!

principles.ruleOfThumb: In possession: at least 3 options: short to feet 5-10 m away and out of the nearest marker's reach; down the line; and back or inside to a player facing forward who can switch play. There is no offside from a throw-in, so runners may start beyond the last defender. Out of possession: stay at least 2 m from the thrower; stand goal-side of the nearest receivers; one player blocks the line; track runners, because the offside trap doesn't apply.

why.standard: Throw-ins happen dozens of times a game, and good options keep the ball while poor ones hand it straight back.
why.kid: A throw-in happens dozens of times a game. Give the thrower a real choice and you keep the ball.

principles.commonMistake: Everyone standing still and marked, so the thrower has to launch it down the line to nobody.

principles.name: Penalty rebounds

summary.standard: At a penalty, everyone except the taker and the keeper waits outside the box and the arc, behind the spot, ready to follow in any rebound.
summary.kid: Penalty? Wait outside the box, then rush in for rebounds.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Everyone except the kicker and the keeper stays on the field, outside the box, behind the penalty spot and at least 9.15 m from it (outside the arc). Target spots are on the box line either side of the arc (x about 16.5, y about 26-29 and 39-42, defaults). Defenders take the inside spots, goal-side of the attackers.

why.standard: Rebounds from saves and the woodwork are common, and the first player to react usually wins them.
why.kid: Saves and posts spit the ball back out. The first player to react usually wins it. Follow every shot.

principles.commonMistake: Stepping into the box or the arc before the kick is taken, which can get the penalty retaken.

principles.name: Youth 7v7 build-out line

summary.standard: In U9-U10 7v7, when the opponent's keeper has the ball, retreat behind the build-out line until the ball is in play, which gives young teams room to pass out from the back.
summary.kid: Their keeper has the ball? Go back behind the build-out line.

principles.ruleOfThumb: When the opposing keeper holds the ball, or at their goal kick, retreat behind the build-out line until the ball is in play. The keeper may not punt. Offside applies only between the build-out line and the goal line. Formations: 1-2-3-1 or 1-3-2-1 for 7v7; 1-3-2-3 or 1-3-3-2 for 9v9. Sources place the line differently, so the app makes it configurable.

why.standard: The line encourages young teams to pass out from the back instead of kicking long.
why.kid: The line gives young teams room to pass out from the back instead of kicking long.

principles.commonMistake: Pressing the keeper inside the build-out zone before the ball is in play.

principles.name: Scan before you receive
principles.who: Every player about to receive the ball

summary.standard: Check over your shoulders before the ball reaches you, so you already know your next pass when it arrives.
summary.kid: Look around before the ball gets to you.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Take several looks in the last seconds before you receive: professionals average about 0.44 looks per second, about 3 in the last 10 s, and look most before a long forward pass (sourced). In the app the watch before the freeze is your look; the engine does not rate scanning.

why.standard: The picture you take before the ball arrives decides how quickly and how well you can pass it on.
why.kid: Look before the ball arrives. Then you already know your pass. You play faster and better.

principles.commonMistake: Watching only the ball, then having to stop and look up after it arrives.

principles.name: Play forward when it is on

summary.standard: Pick the forward pass when it is safe. If it is not on, go around by switching the play, or back.
summary.kid: If a forward pass is safe, play it.

principles.ruleOfThumb: If a good (green) forward pass scores within 10 points of the best pass (default), a safe square or back pass is too safe: it grades B or C at most (its score is capped at 79, default).

why.standard: Every forward pass that keeps the ball takes the team nearer goal, while a sideways pass gives the defence time to get set.
why.kid: Every forward pass that keeps the ball takes you nearer goal. A sideways pass lets their defence get set.

principles.commonMistake: Passing sideways or back because it feels safe, even when a teammate ahead is free.

principles.name: Find the free player

summary.standard: Pass to the teammate with time and space, not to one squeezed between opponents.
summary.kid: Pass to a teammate with no one near.

principles.ruleOfThumb: Pressure on the receiver comes from an oval that reaches 9 m in front of them and 3 m behind (sourced). Below 0.15 the receiver is free; 0.6 or more means under pressure (defaults).

why.standard: A free player can control the ball, look up and play on, while a tightly marked one is likely to lose it.
why.kid: A free teammate can control it, look up, and play on. A tightly watched one will likely lose it.

principles.commonMistake: Passing to the nearest teammate even though a defender is standing right next to them.

principles.name: Pass through a clear lane

summary.standard: A pass needs a clear lane: no defender within reach of the line, and none who can get across before the ball arrives.
summary.kid: If a defender is in the way, don't pass there.

principles.ruleOfThumb: The engine works out the chance that each defender cuts the pass out: a body block by anyone within about 1 m of the line (default), and a race to the ball at 5 m/s after a 0.7 s reaction (sourced). A lane safety of 0.8 or more is good and below 0.5 is cut out (defaults); the defender in the way is ringed.

why.standard: A pass that is cut out loses the ball, often with their players already running at your goal.
why.kid: A pass that is cut out loses the ball. Often their players are already running at your goal when it happens.

principles.commonMistake: Passing to a teammate who looks free while a defender stands in the lane between you.

principles.name: Break lines with your pass
principles.who: Defenders and midfielders on the ball

summary.standard: Move the ball between and beyond their players, and count the opponents your pass takes out of the game.
summary.kid: Pass past their players, not in front of them.

principles.ruleOfThumb: An opponent is taken out when they were nearer their own goal than the ball before the pass and are no longer after it (Impect's bypassed-opponents test). The engine names the line the pass gets through: their forwards, their midfield or their back line.

why.standard: Every opponent a pass gets past has to turn and run back before they can defend again.
why.kid: Every opponent your pass gets past must turn and run back. Until they do, they cannot defend.

principles.commonMistake: Passing in front of their midfield, where the receiver has opponents facing them.

principles.name: Switch play to the free side
principles.who: Defenders and midfielders on the ball

summary.standard: When the ball side is crowded, move the ball across to the far side, where a teammate holds the width.
summary.kid: Crowded here? Send it to the free side.

principles.ruleOfThumb: A switch goes at least 25 m across into the far half (default) and is safe (green). The drills crowd the ball side and leave your far full-back or winger free.

why.standard: Defenders slide toward the ball, so the far side is where the space and the free player are.
why.kid: Defenders slide toward the ball. So the space and the free teammate are on the far side.

principles.commonMistake: Forcing the ball into the crowded side because it is the way you are facing.

principles.name: Play to the correct foot

summary.standard: Pass to the foot away from the defender when the receiver can turn, and to the near foot when they are pressed; lead a runner.
summary.kid: Pass to the foot far from the defender.

principles.ruleOfThumb: The engine aims the pass 0.5-1 m away from the receiver's nearest marker (default) and shows the aim in the reveal. It is graded only from v2, which needs body shape.

why.standard: A pass to the safe foot lets the receiver shield the ball or turn away from the defender.
why.kid: Pass to the foot away from the defender. Your teammate can shield the ball or turn away safely.

principles.commonMistake: Passing straight at the receiver's feet with a defender tight on that side.

learnMore.label: Soccer Coach Weekly: back-foot and front-foot passing

principles.name: Pass into space ahead of a runner

summary.standard: Play into space when your runner will get there first; play to feet when the receiver is marked or coming short.
summary.kid: Runner in space? Pass in front of them.

principles.ruleOfThumb: A pass into space is on when your runner wins the race to it (a share of 0.6 or more, default) and was level with or behind their last defender when you played it.

why.standard: A pass into space lets your teammate run onto the ball at full speed instead of stopping to receive it.
why.kid: A pass into space lets your teammate run onto it at full speed. They never have to stop and wait.

principles.commonMistake: Passing to where the runner is now, so they have to stop and wait for the ball.

principles.name: Pick a receiver who can turn

summary.standard: Prefer a teammate who can turn and face goal. A player with their back to goal and a marker tight behind will have to play it back.
summary.kid: Pick a teammate who can turn and face goal.

principles.ruleOfThumb: The receiver can turn with 6 m or more of free run toward goal and pressure below 0.3; pressure of 0.6 or more means under pressure (defaults).

why.standard: A receiver who can turn keeps the attack moving forward, while one who must play it back slows it down.
why.kid: A teammate who can turn keeps the attack going forward. One who must pass it back slows everything down.

principles.commonMistake: Passing into a teammate who has a defender right behind them and no way to turn.

principles.name: Never pass across your own goal

summary.standard: In your own third, never play a sideways pass across the front of your goal unless it is completely safe.
summary.kid: Never pass across the front of your own goal.

principles.ruleOfThumb: The pass starts and ends in our own third, goes mostly sideways (at least 15 m across and more than 1.5 times as far across as forward), crosses the area in front of our goal, and its lane is not completely safe (below 0.9): the engine marks it as a danger (defaults).

why.standard: If a pass across your own goal is cut out, the opponent has the ball right in front of your goal.
why.kid: If a pass across your own goal is cut out, they get the ball right by your goal.

principles.commonMistake: Playing the easy square pass to the other centre-back while their striker waits in between.
